passage: Manoj's tower of steel tumblers crashed across the kitchen floor of the Pune flat, and Pradeep shouted, "Enough! Pick them up now!" Manoj froze, then howled. "You wanted the tower to reach the shelf." "It fell," Manoj whispered. Pradeep rubbed his back until the sobs slowed. Then they gathered the tumblers together, one clink at a time.

passage: Sit, beta. Your Bhavna aunty will tell you about Deepak, my friend from engineering college in Nagpur, back when we were twenty. A year ago I could never have written this. I used to keep a list of things I couldn't say to anyone I lived with, in case they went cold on me for days.
Last month I told you I resented how often your family visits. My hands were shaking. You didn't snap or go quiet. You said, "That's hard to hear, but I'm glad you told me," and then you asked what would help.
That's what you do. The same calm on bad Tuesdays as on good Sundays. Because I don't have to guard every word, I've started telling you small scary things too: that I want to change jobs, that I cry at weddings.
Thank you for making honesty feel safe here.
Love,
Urmila
